summary: Ashgrove passes the growth test: revenue rose from USD 765.1m in 2023 to USD 955.8m in 2025, a 24.9% two-year increase versus the 21.7% industry median, consistent with management’s letter. It fails the new-product test: products launched since 2023 supplied 22.9% of 2025 revenue, below the 29.2% industry median, and management’s insistence that research spending has never been cut is not corroborated by that share, while a customer calls the product “a commodity.” It passes the margin test: the 2025 operating margin was 13.4% versus the 9.4% industry median, though it has slipped from 16.1% in 2023 and 14.5% in 2024.

Revenue rose 18.3% from 2023 to 2025 versus an industry median of 11.5%, so point 1 passes; management’s “18% more than 2023” is consistent with that. Products launched since 2023 supplied 24.7% of 2025 revenue versus a 19.6% median, so point 2 passes. The 2025 operating margin was 12.6% versus a 10.3% median, up from 10.6% in 2023 and 11.4% in 2024, so point 5 passes. The scuttlebutt is less flattering—a customer calls the product a commodity and a former manager describes executive conflict—but those comments do not overturn the measured growth, new-product share, and margin advantages.

Revenue rose 21.1% from 2023 to 2025, ahead of the 14.8% industry median, so the growth verdict passes. Products launched since 2023 supplied 28.5% of 2025 revenue versus 21.0% for the industry median, supporting the new-product verdict, though one customer describes the product as a commodity. The 2025 operating margin of 13.6% was above the 11.9% industry median and improved from 12.3% in 2023 and 13.3% in 2024; management’s claim of sustained long-term research spending is not quantified in these figures.

Cobalt Holdings grew revenue 8.0% from 2023 to 2025, below the 11.5% industry median, so the growth verdict is a fail even though management frames the 8% increase as a strength. New products launched since 2023 supplied 26.4% of 2025 revenue against a 19.6% median, supporting the pass on innovation, and a customer's two-year requalification comment reinforces that stickiness. Operating margin of 14.2% also beats the 10.3% median, though it has slipped from 16.0% in 2023 and 15.1% in 2024, so the pass comes with a declining trend rather than a widening lead.

Copperfield passes point 1 on revenue growth: sales rose from USD 713.2m in 2023 to USD 912.1m in 2025, a 27.9% increase against an industry median of 20.1%, which is consistent with management's letter claiming roughly 28% growth. It passes point 2 because products launched since 2023 supplied 32.9% of 2025 revenue versus a 27.0% median, giving some support to the letter's claim that research spending has never been cut. Point 5 passes as well, with a 2025 operating margin of 18.0% above the 15.1% industry median and up from 15.1% in 2023 and 16.1% in 2024, although the letter's praise of its "deep bench" and teamwork is assertion rather than evidence of cause. The foundry buyer's remark that switching away would take two years of requalification supports the customer stickiness underpinning these margins.

Driftwood fails point 1 because two-year revenue growth was 8.6%, below the 12.0% industry median, even though management’s letter describes the gain as 9%. It passes point 2 because products launched since 2023 supplied 26.7% of 2025 revenue, above the 18.5% median, and passes point 5 because its 2025 operating margin of 13.6% exceeded the 11.4% median and had risen from 12.5% in 2023 and 13.3% in 2024. The scuttlebutt adds a caveat—a customer says it buys on price among four suppliers and a former manager reports executive conflict—but it does not overturn the fixed verdicts.

Dunmore's revenue rose from USD 772.9m in 2023 to USD 950.6m in 2025, a 23.0% gain above the 18.9% industry median, so point 1 passes. Point 2 fails because products launched since 2023 supplied 18.3% of 2025 revenue versus a 26.6% industry median, even though management calls research the engine and says it funds it accordingly. Point 5 passes because the 2025 operating margin was 15.0%, above the 12.5% median and up from 13.6% in 2023 and 13.9% in 2024.

Revenue climbed from USD 304.5m in 2023 to USD 388.2m in 2025, a 27.5% two-year gain against an industry median of 21.7%, so growth earns a pass, and the USD 223.5m booked in 2026 to date is consistent with that pace. New-product share fails: products launched since 2023 supplied only 23.0% of 2025 revenue versus a 29.2% median, which sits awkwardly with management's line that research is "the engine of this company," and a customer's comment that buyers simply take whoever is cheapest that quarter points to limited pricing power. The margin test passes on 2025's 11.7% operating margin against a 9.4% median, extending a steady rise from 10.5% in 2023 and 11.3% in 2024.

Emberly passes point 1 because revenue grew 26.2% from 2023 to 2025, above the 18.9% industry median, and management’s “26% more than 2023” claim is consistent with that. It passes point 2 because products launched since 2023 supplied 31.8% of 2025 revenue versus a 26.6% median, and passes point 5 because its 15.4% 2025 operating margin beat the 12.5% median. The margin has nonetheless slipped from 18.1% in 2023 and 16.4% in 2024, and management’s qualitative claims about its sales bench and research commitment are assertions rather than evidence.

Everline passes point 1 because revenue grew 19.0% from 2023 to 2025 versus an 11.5% industry median, and passes point 2 because products launched since 2023 supplied 28.5% of 2025 revenue versus 19.6% for the industry. It fails point 5 because its 2025 operating margin was 6.3% against a 10.3% industry median, even though it improved from 5.2% in 2023 and 5.4% in 2024. Management's letter praises gross margin, a different measure, while customer comments on line performance and the former manager's account of a cohesive top team are supportive color but do not change these verdicts.

Falcrest passes point 1: revenue grew 26.9% from 2023 to 2025, above the 21.7% industry median. It also passes point 2, with products launched since 2023 supplying 37.7% of 2025 revenue versus a 29.2% industry median. Point 5 fails because the 2025 operating margin was 6.3% against a 9.4% industry median, and while margin improved from 4.6% in 2023 and 5.7% in 2024, management’s cost-control claim does not close that gap.

Fernhill passes point 1 because revenue rose from USD 559.1m in 2023 to USD 639.4m in 2025, a 14.4% gain versus the 9.8% industry median, and management’s “14% more than 2023” claim is consistent with that figure. It passes point 2 because products launched since 2023 supplied 23.8% of 2025 revenue versus a 15.2% median, and point 5 because the 2025 operating margin of 11.4% exceeded the 8.3% median and improved from 9.1% in 2023 and 10.7% in 2024. The scuttlebutt—price-driven buying and executive friction—is a caution, but it does not overturn these three pass verdicts.

Granite Group passes point 1 because revenue rose from USD 305.2m in 2023 to USD 375.3m in 2025, a 23.0% two-year gain that tops the 16.2% industry median. It fails point 2: products launched since 2023 supplied 19.7% of 2025 revenue, below the 24.2% industry median, so management’s emphasis on research as the company’s engine is not yet reflected in new-product contribution. It passes point 5 with a 2025 operating margin of 19.7% versus the 16.8% median, even though that margin has eased from 21.2% in 2023. The customer’s praise for performance and the former manager’s view of teamwork support the competitive and management picture, but they do not close the new-product gap.

Halcyon's revenue grew 7.7% from 2023 to 2025, below the 12.0% industry median, so the growth verdict is FAIL. New products launched since 2023 supplied 13.0% of 2025 revenue versus an 18.5% median, making the new-product verdict FAIL, and management's talk of sustained research spending does not demonstrate commercial traction. The 2025 operating margin was 9.5% against an 11.4% median—better than 8.4% in 2023 and 9.4% in 2024, but still below the industry—so the margin verdict is FAIL. Positive scuttlebutt on switching costs and teamwork does not offset those measured shortfalls.

Hollins passes point 1 because revenue grew 19.3% from 2023 to 2025 (437.6 to 522.0), above the 16.2% industry median, and management’s letter noting 19% growth is consistent with that. It passes point 2 because products launched since 2023 supplied 28.3% of 2025 revenue versus the 24.2% median, and point 5 because the 20.5% operating margin exceeded the 16.8% median after improving from 18.3% in 2023 and 19.6% in 2024. The customer quote about unmatched performance and the former manager’s comment on a trusting top team support the competitive and management picture, though management’s qualitative claims about people and research spending are assertions rather than measured evidence.

Revenue grew 14.4% from 2023 to 2025, below the 21.7% industry median, so Point 1 fails even though management presents the 14% increase positively. Products launched since 2023 supplied 23.4% of 2025 revenue versus 29.2% for the industry median, so Point 2 fails despite the emphasis on research spending. The 2025 operating margin was 5.8% against a 9.4% industry median, so Point 5 fails even with the improving 3.6% to 5.8% margin history and cost-control comments.

Juniper’s two-year revenue growth of 14.5%, from 2023 to 2025, lags the 21.7% industry median, so point 1 fails; management’s letter reports 15%, slightly above the figure shown but still below the median. New products launched since 2023 supplied 35.7% of 2025 revenue versus 29.2% for the median, passing point 2, and a customer’s comment that switching would require two years of requalification supports that traction. The 2025 operating margin was 11.6% against a 9.4% median, up from 10.5% in 2023 and 11.1% in 2024, so point 5 passes.

Kestrel’s two-year revenue growth of 4.2%, from USD 555.0m in 2023 to USD 578.6m in 2025, trails the 9.8% industry median, so point 1 fails despite management’s broadly consistent “4% more than 2023” claim. Point 2 passes because products launched since 2023 supplied 24.2% of 2025 revenue versus a 15.2% median, and point 5 passes because the 10.0% operating margin exceeds the 8.3% median and has improved from 9.0% in 2023. The customer’s two-year requalification comment supports switching costs, while the former manager’s comment supports the teamwork claim but does not alter the financial verdicts.

Lindale passes the two growth tests: revenue rose 13.6% from 2023 to 2025 against a 9.8% industry median, and products launched since 2023 supplied 24.1% of 2025 revenue versus 15.2% for the median peer. It fails the operating-margin test, with 4.5% in 2025 below the 8.3% industry median and down from 6.2% in 2023 and 5.7% in 2024. Management’s talk of long-term research investment and gross-margin strength does not offset that operating-profit shortfall, and the customer’s two-year requalification comment supports stickiness but not pricing power.

Northwind earns a pass on revenue growth because 2023-to-2025 revenue rose 24.7%, above the 20.1% industry median. It also earns a pass on new-product share because products launched since 2023 supplied 35.2% of 2025 revenue, above the 27.0% median. It fails on operating margin because 2025 margin was 12.8% versus a 15.1% median, and the trend weakened from 15.5% in 2023 to 13.6% in 2024 to 12.8% in 2025; management’s long-term research and quality comments are assertions, not evidence, and the former manager’s account of executive conflict clashes with the letter’s “one team” claim.
